items.question: How do you understand the stage AI has reached today?
items.object: AI’s current stage of development
items.answer: For me, I may not see clearly what counts as the first half and what counts as the second half; that definition has never been especially clear to me. But AI has indeed entered a stage where people are less worried about whether AI can do something, and more worried about whether the task has been well defined. That is a major difference. For example, a year ago—perhaps early last year—when I was at Anthropic, people might still worry: OpenAI’s reasoning is so strong; can we catch up, and how likely are we to surpass it? People were very concerned about that. Now, at least among Gemini, OpenAI, and Anthropic, I do not think any of them truly worries that it cannot catch up. I think the harder thing now is figuring out what to do. It is a bet, but it also requires a great deal of human insight.

items.question: How do you interpret the narrowing public benchmark scores of models from Gemini, OpenAI, and Anthropic?
items.object: Public benchmarks as measures of differences among leading AI models
items.answer: In users’ actual experience, you can still feel differences among the models from the three companies. But the difficult thing is that, in the past, the differences were also visible on paper. By “on paper,” I mean there are many public benchmarks and evaluation standards. Previously people could look at SWE-bench, for example. They might compare a simpler AIME and a harder AMO in math. At the time, you could tell from the numbers: this model seemed a bit better at reasoning, that one at coding, this one at something else. Now they are all relatively close on paper. If you look at SWE-bench, perhaps a better model is one or two percentage points higher than a worse one, but everyone is around 80 percent. A slightly higher or lower number there is mainly noise rather than signal.

items.question: How do you understand the unexpected ways internet pretraining data can shape a model’s coding ability?

items.question: How do you understand the constraints that make it harder for large companies like Google to release experimental AI products than for independent developers?
items.object: Large-company constraints on releasing experimental AI products
items.answer: I think that once a company gets large, its burdens grow too. As a researcher, we can make products that look interesting and distinctive. But once I release a product publicly, there are many things to take responsibility for. First, you cannot launch it and tell all users: you need to buy another computer for this, otherwise it may get every permission on your computer and crash your system. As a large company, Google cannot ship such a product, right? So you need to spend a lot of time polishing the product, ensure it carries no legal risks, ensure users will not damage your brand, and if you ship it, you may have to allocate fairly fixed resources to serve the model or product line. Large companies carry many burdens. But individuals do not care: it is an open-source project—so what if my code is garbage? Come write it with me.

items.question: How do you see the prospect of training models with finite context but using nearly infinite context at inference time in 2026?
items.object: Training with finite context and using nearly infinite context at inference time
items.answer: In terms of model capability, I like to say this slogan: “train with finite context, use as infinite context.” In other words, train with a finite context length but use a very long, even nearly infinite, context length at inference time. I think there is an opportunity to achieve this this year. Once it is achieved, it will unlock many applications. In the simplest example, a model could interact with you continuously and keep acquiring information about you; while running, based on the current situation and your conversations, it could discard information it considers unimportant. Then it becomes the personal assistant people dream of. Technically, I think this will be achieved this year one way or another. What people have not reached consensus on is how to achieve it. Clearly there are many technical routes. We are more at the stage of trying which route can work. Several routes may work, and then we will need experiments to measure which is most efficient in common long-term user scenarios. We are at that stage, not at a stage where people have no ideas. People have ideas, but need to determine which one is the final idea.

items.question: How do you understand the roles of data, compute, and algorithms in improving model capability?

items.question: How do you explain the rapid development of AI coding capabilities and products?

items.answer: I think coding has two biggest advantages. First, its reward signal is easy to define. For example, a software-engineering task may be: I need to write code implementing a feature. The feature should yield certain outputs for certain inputs. That is easy to test. So the reward signal is clear: if inputs and outputs match, the implementation succeeded; if not, it did not. That is only one example. In code-related work, there are many, many well-defined reward signals like this. The other major advantage is that coding data has a very natural foundation. That foundation is GitHub. GitHub brings together code written over the past several decades by many, many high-quality programmers. Starting from that code, you can construct very, very many environments. I think those two things explain, from the model’s perspective, why coding can be done well. items.question: How did you come to understand your research on non-Hermitian quantum systems as a paradigm update?

items.answer: Its essence is studying the behavior of open quantum systems—quantum systems that exchange with the outside world. Then we found something puzzling. At first we tried to study certain topological phenomena in open quantum systems, and found that the theoretical result calculated analytically simply would not match the numerical result. More precisely, the analytical result assumed periodic boundary conditions—for example, a system on a ring or on the surface of a tire. Numerically, because it is closer to real situations, one calculates an open boundary, such as the behavior of material in a box. We found the two results simply would not match, and tried to understand why. Later we found that a basic paradigm previously used to describe Hermitian systems, the so-called Bloch wave—assuming a system's eigenstates are linear combinations of sine and cosine waves—this assumption actually breaks down, becomes wrong, in non-Hermitian systems. What we later found was that energy eigenstates in non-Hermitian systems may all accumulate at one edge of the system. We systematically established a framework for describing this: how the eigenstates of an open-boundary non-Hermitian system should be described, and then some dynamics of its time evolution. That was the work at the time. Since it was a paradigm update, it later generated many follow-up works. But I changed fields, so I did not continue in that direction.

items.question: How do you understand the apparent conflict between the classical butterfly effect and the linear evolution of quantum systems?
items.object: The butterfly effect in classical and quantum systems
items.answer:
The familiar butterfly effect is actually classical physics: the famous example is that a butterfly in South America flaps its wings, and half a month later a typhoon occurs in North America. Mathematically, it means that if you make a very small perturbation at the initial time and measure how large its effect is in the future—you find that the perturbation's change grows exponentially. That is its mathematical description in the classical butterfly effect.

But what people found puzzling was how this could exist in a quantum system. As I just said, an isolated quantum system evolves unitarily; it is a very linear process. In a sense, if the angle between one state vector and another is not very large initially, after evolution that angle should not change. So how can an initially tiny difference between states grow exponentially large in the future? In quantum mechanics it seems impossible. But as I also said, the world is quantum microscopically and classical macroscopically; the two are continuous, so how can one have this and the other not? That is what people tried to understand.

Later people developed a better understanding: when discussing macroscopic effects in quantum systems, you should not discuss the change between two states, but changes in so-called local observables. Those correspond to the changes you see in classical physics.

items.question: How do you understand the claim that language models are black boxes?

items.answer: I see these two things as both falling within the broad category of models using tools, interacting with environments, and interacting with different models and people. In this category, the point we had completed in the past was one-stop coding. That involves both tools and interaction with environments—the environment being a virtual machine, or your own computer. This then grows horizontally into different use cases. AI research is another scenario in that horizontal space. It is not only a new scenario horizontally; vertically, it also makes the scale of the task longer. Because completing a code completion might be very quick, whereas carrying out a complete AI research project or computer-science research is a very long process. So it is like a T shape: expansion horizontally and extension vertically.

items.question: Why do you favor post-training approaches for enabling models to perform long-context tasks?
items.object: Pre-training and post-training approaches to long-context tasks
items.answer: I probably cannot talk in too much detail, but broadly, some approaches come from pre-training. From the pre-training perspective, some approaches are like sparse attention. DeepSeek, for example, has done some work on that, and there is much academic work too. From the post-training perspective, there are also post-training approaches, such as the strong context-management ability of things like Cursor that you use every day: it can let a model decide, hey, this middle section is unimportant, so throw it away; that section is important, so save it in a file and retrieve it later. Broadly, both approaches are being researched. Their concrete implementation details go beyond the examples I just gave; those were relatively public examples. Of course every company has its own little secrets in the implementation details, but ultimately everyone will come to know them. I personally spend more time on the post-training part, first because I do not formally spend work time on pre-training; pre-training is more an interest of mine, something I want to learn about. But I have not done much work on it myself. On the other hand, I think the post-training approach fits my own understanding of this problem better. My understanding is the thing I have been saying: can we train with short context but have it do long-context tasks? These pre-training approaches fundamentally still require long-context training.

items.question: How do you understand the roles of Llama and Gemini 3 in Gemini’s market breakthrough?
items.object: Gemini’s market breakthrough through Llama and Gemini 3
items.answer: In terms of actual results, I think two things gave Gemini a major turning point and made it a significant player in the market: Llama and Gemini 3, one after the other. I think if there had only been Gemini 3, the effect might not have been as good as it is now. When your market share is under ten percent, whether your model is a little better or worse spreads too slowly. But Llama accomplished something: it became hugely popular in the market, and large numbers of people downloaded the Gemini app. Then Gemini 3 was released right afterward and retained those users. So now it has become a significant player. Without Gemini landing such a punch, OpenAI would have been in a very comfortable position: its market share was already so high that changes in model capability might not have affected it that much. And honestly, I think that when ordinary people actually use models, their perception of the model's capabilities is really weak. The vast majority of people do not even use the O-series models; most people just use the regular GPT ones. Right, so I think for Gemini, having Llama drive up volume and then Gemini 3 retain users is very important.

items.question: How do you understand Google's ability to catch up with OpenAI in chatbots?
items.object: Google's organizational progress and OpenAI's effect on its chatbot response
items.answer: I think, first of all, Google's technical reserves have always been sufficient. There have always been enough people. And organizationally, things later became clearer and clearer: there was a better framework for everyone to work together on this. So there may gradually have been some progress. And, in a sense, as an outsider, I think OpenAI saved Google's life. Because people had always worried that chatbots might completely replace search. If that had really happened, Google would have been in a very painful position, right? But fortunately OpenAI did it first, making Google realize it mattered, yet it did not take it all the way or push it to the extreme. items.question: How do you explain why OpenAI’s chatbots have not completely replaced search?
items.object: Chatbots’ ability to replace search and OpenAI’s execution
items.answer: I think both are true. First, the current chatbot mode of interaction will not completely eat search. Its advantage over search, as we said earlier, is its strong interactivity: you can ask follow-up questions, and it can help condense very complex information. That is where it is powerful. In those use cases, it really will pull users away from search. But search also has some very dumb use cases: for very simple things, you simply do not want to spend the time on a chatbot. For example, if I just want to buy rice, I search for buying rice and that is it. Why would I have to ask ChatGPT which one is better, wait while it spins for ages, get a link, click it, then go to a webpage to buy it? There is no need. So in terms of actual usage, its current form is not enough to completely eat search. And from another angle, perhaps it also did not take chatbots to their absolute peak. It really let others—Google—catch up with it.

What Google is especially good at is finding an extremely simple product form, where everybody’s products look the same, and then relentlessly competing on technology until you cannot outdo it. items.question: How do you understand the essential differences between pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning?
items.object: The relationship between pre-training, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning
items.answer: I think it is hard to state, from a purely technical perspective, what the essential difference is between pre-training, supervised learning/SFT, and RL. Pre-training and SFT themselves do not have much essential difference either: you simply treat the data you obtain as ground truth, treat it as the expert output, and move toward the distribution of that expert output. Reinforcement learning is perhaps a broader level: the output is not initially supplied by a given expert; I generate some things myself, some results are good and some are bad, and I move toward the good ones and away from the bad ones. So in a sense, pre-training and SFT are subsets of reinforcement learning. But they are indeed different things in the current era. To me, the biggest difference is in the data. Pre-training data needs a sufficiently good distribution—broad enough, or sufficiently aligned with the range you want to cover—but its quality need not be extremely high. Post-training is the reverse: its distribution may be narrow, but the quality requirements for the data it has are extremely high. So to me, at present their most essential difference is still the difference in data distribution, not a difference in algorithms or training paradigms.

items.question: What do you think it takes for an organization to do AI systematically?
items.object: Doing AI systematically
items.answer: I think there are several aspects. At the system level, it requires a scientific attitude: you need to clearly understand exactly what assumptions you have made. When I make a change, what factors are associated with it and which are not? That is at the organizational level. At the human level, people need to be reliable—very responsible. Every system, every evaluation framework, is easy to hack, because you can always do things that make your metrics look very good. But a trustworthy or grounded person will ask whether, if what they did looks good, it is truly good at scale, and whether they missed factors along the way. So doing things systematically sounds like one phrase, but actually doing it is very complicated. There will be a lot of resistance, because it goes against human nature. Each person's individual instinct may be to make the thing they made look better. But for a company or organization, the most beneficial thing is to make the entire company's system extremely solid and rigorous.

items.question: What do you think responsible algorithm evaluation requires in a large-scale AI research organization?
items.object: Responsible algorithm evaluation within a large-scale AI research organization
items.answer: I can give a perhaps rather odd example. Say I am doing bridge learning: I may produce an algorithm that performs better than others, but perhaps the more crucial question is whether I can maintain equally good stability at real, large scale. And whether my result is better than others' because I used different data, more training FLOPs, or more sampling FLOPs. In the final large production run, what exactly is my limiting factor, and which metric should I look at? These are things researchers themselves need a good understanding of—how the system works—and a sense of responsibility to the company in order to do. Otherwise it is easy, for example, to be better than others when you count training, but worse when you count training plus sampling. You can always choose to show only training. items.answer: I think that is a very controversial question. Some organizations are more top-down and some more bottom-up. A natural question is which of those is better at stimulating innovation. The traditional view is that bottom-up is necessary for innovation, because people need freedom; only when individuals have freedom can there be innovation. But it turns out a completely bottom-up approach does not work either, because then it becomes chaotic. At least that is my impression from what I have learned. It was chaotic. People did not even know what use the thing they were doing had, and that may not be good either. So perhaps you need a person or a small collective that can blend those two things somewhat. That is why I think whether an organization operates well may look like an organizational issue, but ultimately it is a question of the technical leader. Does that technical leader have the qualities to keep the organization operating steadily? Because the best state is often the most unstable one; it can very easily collapse toward a bad state. items.question: How do you assess the tradeoffs between GPUs and Google's TPUs at large commercial scale?
items.object: GPUs and Google's TPUs at large commercial scale
items.answer: From a pure hardware perspective, it is hard to say any hardware is truly good or bad, especially at large commercial scale. Fundamentally, setting hardware differences aside, the biggest practical difference between GPUs and TPUs is that GPUs have a better open-source ecosystem. TPUs do not. But at large commercial scale, that is not really a problem. If Google itself uses TPUs, it will naturally spend time building the infrastructure. If you run only a thousand cards, that infrastructure may be a major burden, but if you run a cluster with hundreds of thousands of cards, building it is not such a big deal. So in actual large-scale commercial use, neither is simply better. But they do differ in design philosophy. For example, at least with the Hopper generation of H-class GPUs—I have not used the more recent generations much—a pod may have only eight cards, and every pair of those eight can interconnect. NVLink is very fast, so that pod has almost no communication bound. TPUs may take the opposite approach: they give up all-to-all pairwise interconnection between cards, but put as many cards as possible into one large rack. They have this 3D-torus design: each card connects only to its nearest neighbors in three directions, but the entire cluster can form one large torus. If your compiler or scheduling logic is good enough, you can exploit that. In effect, you get a larger storage space and reduce many communication bounds.

items.question: How do you use your 24-hour reinforcement-learning interview assignment to judge whether someone is reliable in their work?
items.object: A 24-hour reinforcement-learning project as an interview test of reliability
items.answer: Everyone has their own ways of judging, and of course I have some tricks of my own. I once had an interview question. I can tell everyone about it; it should not be a secret. The interview question is very simple. I ask the person to complete a reinforcement-learning project from zero to one within 24 hours. They choose the model themselves. I tell them what resources they have, and they choose the model, data, and algorithm, then train the model. After the 24 hours, we have an hour-long discussion. In the AI era, this is not that hard. Before AI, it would have been impossible; nobody could finish it in 24 hours. But with AI it is particularly easy, because AI can help you do the whole package. Why do it anyway? There are many reasons. Two reasons for designing it this way are: first, I think in this era there is no point still testing, for example, whether someone writes code well, because most people do not write code themselves. What matters more is whether they can use AI effectively, and that is one aspect the question tests. The second aspect is that there is a trap. If you let AI do everything, but do not make a serious effort to understand what it did for you, you will be exposed in that hour-long discussion. That is a place where people fail. So the other thing it tests is whether you have genuinely formed a collaboration with AI, or simply handed everything over to it. That is something I personally value. That is also part of whether the person is reliable in how they work. Of course, the design of the question itself also has a somewhat dark little twist: why make it 24 hours? To see how much the person values the opportunity. If they are willing to stay up enough, they can make it through those 24 hours. If they cannot, it can only mean they did not value the opportunity that much.

items.question: How do you assess the opportunities in AI for people younger than you who are choosing what to work on?

items.answer: I think purely doing language models is no longer a blue ocean. I think it is too late. The last train has already left. I feel that when I entered the field, that was the last train. And after I entered the field there have certainly been newcomers, but I think they no longer had the opportunity to encounter opportunities that good. The chance to do something in a group that was not so small yet not so large—they are unlikely to encounter such an opportunity. But AI is a very large direction, and language models are only a very small part of it. There are many other things—for example, multimodal generation may have many opportunities. So for people young enough, working on the hottest thing right now may not be the right choice. Doing things nobody has done yet may be a better choice.
